questions.title: Does “certifying” under La. R.S. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) require a human signature, or can a company certify via an unsigned, automated notice?
questions.question_body: The panel emphasizes that the statute "makes no explicit reference to a signature" and concludes there’s "no reason that a company cannot certify information without a named employee being identified." It distinguishes Benitez v. Elsayed, which flagged the lack of a signature but didn’t hold that alone was fatal. Under Louisiana law, what does “certify” in § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) actually entail? Does certification imply a sworn/attested statement by a specific individual, or can a corporate entity effectively "certify" through an unsigned form email generated by its system?

questions.title: What constitutes “receipt” by the insurer when cancellation notices arrive by email and are processed automatically?
questions.question_body: Section 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) allows the insurer to cancel "[u]pon receipt of such notice" from the premium finance company. Here, APAC’s system emails the notice overnight, a GoAuto web service "listens" and auto-cancels before any human sees the notice, and only later does someone stamp documents. The court relies on Black’s definitions of "receipt/receive" and says the computer’s intake suffices. Is there Louisiana authority on whether server-level or automated-system intake qualifies as "receipt" or "physical possession"? At what point is an emailed cancellation request deemed "received" for purposes of this statute—upon arrival in the insurer’s mail server, successful API call, or human review?

questions.title: Can an APAC employee acting as a courier qualify as a “private carrier” under § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)?
questions.question_body: The district court alternatively reasoned that the APAC employee who physically delivered/stamped notices "fits the definition of private carrier," analogizing to a federal case about railroads. The Fifth Circuit called that "imaginative and unconventional" and didn’t reach it. Under Louisiana law, does the statutory phrase "by depositing...with a private carrier" contemplate commercial carriers (e.g., FedEx/UPS) only, or can an agent/employee of the sender be a "private carrier"? Are there any Louisiana cases or statutory definitions on point for insurance-premium finance cancellations?

questions.title: How does Louisiana’s “strict adherence” doctrine apply—does § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(iv) require listing names/addresses of interested parties or is a general certification enough?
questions.question_body: Strict adherence cases (Delatte, Eaglin, Britten) say any defect renders cancellation ineffective. The statute requires the finance company’s statement to specify "the names and addresses" of interested parties and the date notice was sent to the insured. The sample APAC language quoted here states only that copies were sent to "all persons shown" to have an interest and that proof of mailing is available, without listing names/addresses in the text. Did attachments to the email supply those specifics, and if so, is it enough that they are in attachments rather than in the body of the certification? Under the strict-adherence doctrine, do courts require literal inclusion of each enumerated item (names/addresses, date sent) in the certification itself?

questions.title: When should the Fifth Circuit certify unsettled questions of Louisiana insurance law to the state supreme court?
questions.question_body: The panel declined to certify despite no Louisiana Supreme Court authority on the meaning of “certifying” or “receipt” here, citing Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass’n and warning against overuse of certification. What is the Fifth Circuit’s standard for certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court in Erie cases? Do novelty and statewide importance of insurance-cancellation procedures suffice, or must there be additional factors (e.g., conflicting intermediate appellate decisions, indeterminacy)? Did the court appropriately apply that standard in refusing certification on these statutory-interpretation issues?

questions.title: What standing or cause of action does a third-party accident victim have to challenge policy cancellation and allege insurer bad faith?
questions.question_body: Plaintiff Jenkins was a third-party tort claimant (not an insured) but joined claims against GoAuto and APAC for misrepresentation and breach of good faith/fair dealing based on allegedly ineffective cancellations. The court affirmed dismissal after finding statutory compliance. Under Louisiana law (e.g., the Direct Action Statute, La. R.S. 22:1269, and La. R.S. 22:1973), do duties concerning cancellation notices and representations run to third-party claimants? If the cancellation was effective and coverage lapsed, can a third-party still pursue misrepresentation or bad-faith claims independent of the coverage determination?

questions.title: Does “receipt” by an affiliate or management company count as receipt by the insurer under § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i)?
questions.question_body: Before 2017, printed requests were stored in a filing room belonging to GoAuto Management Services (an affiliate), not GoAuto. Post-2017, a document is taken to a GoAuto employee for a "received" stamp. If email receipt were ignored, would custody by an affiliate constitute the insurer’s "receipt" under the statute? What agency or corporate-law principles (actual/apparent authority, alter ego, common enterprise) would control whether an affiliate’s possession is imputed to the insurer for purposes of statutory "receipt"?

questions.title: If a signature were required, would Louisiana’s UETA or the federal E-SIGN Act make an electronic or stamped signature sufficient—and must it predate cancellation?
questions.question_body: Although the court held no signature is required, APAC stamps a signature after the automated cancellation occurs. Louisiana has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (La. R.S. 9:2601 et seq.). If a signature were deemed necessary to "certify" under § 9:3550(G)(3)(a), would an electronic signature or a post-hoc stamped signature satisfy that requirement? Does § 9:3550 demand that any required signature exist before the insurer may cancel, or could a later signature/ratification cure the timing issue under Louisiana law’s strict-adherence approach?
